stem: You want to list pods in every namespace. Which command is correct?
rationale: `-A` (all namespaces) is the flag; there is no namespace named "all".

stem: A pod does not start. Which command shows its recent events?
rationale: `describe` shows the events, which usually explain scheduling and startup failures; `logs` needs a started container.

stem: Which command lists all resource types available in a cluster?
rationale: `kubectl api-resources` lists every resource type the cluster serves, including Cozystack's custom types.

stem: Which object keeps the desired number of pod replicas running?
rationale: the ReplicaSet (created by a Deployment) keeps the declared number of pod replicas running.

stem: You need an external IP for a service on bare metal Cozystack. Which Service type requests one?
rationale: type LoadBalancer requests an external IP; in Cozystack MetalLB provides these IPs on bare metal.

stem: In Cozystack, how does a virtual machine run?

options.text: On a separate hypervisor cluster outside Kubernetes
As a Kubernetes pod managed by KubeVirt
As a systemd service on the node

rationale: KubeVirt runs each VM inside a pod (with QEMU); a VM is a Kubernetes workload.

stem: Which field of a manifest holds the desired state of the object?
rationale: `spec` declares the desired state; `metadata` holds identity, `kind` and `apiVersion` select the type.

stem: Which command validates a manifest without creating resources?
rationale: `--dry-run=server` sends the manifest to the API server for validation without persisting anything.

stem: A managed application in Cozystack (for example a database) generates connection credentials. Where does it deliver them?

options.text: In a ConfigMap in the platform namespace
In a generated Secret in the tenant namespace

rationale: managed apps deliver credentials in generated Secrets; the tenant kubeconfig is also built from a Secret (module M2).

stem: What is a Helm release?

options.text: A version of the Helm binary
One installed instance of a chart in a cluster
A Git tag in the chart repository

rationale: a release is one installed instance of a chart; one chart can produce many releases with different values.

stem: What does the `--install` flag add to `helm upgrade`?

options.text: It forces a reinstall of every pod
It installs the release if it does not exist yet
It upgrades all releases in the cluster
It validates values without applying them

rationale: `upgrade --install` is idempotent — it installs when the release is absent and upgrades when it exists.

stem: What does the READY column of `kubectl get hr -A` tell you?

options.text: Whether the pod images were pulled
Whether the HelmRelease is reconciled and healthy
Whether the Git repository is reachable

rationale: READY True means the HelmRelease is reconciled and healthy; False sends you to MESSAGE and `kubectl describe hr`.

stem: What happens when a HelmRelease is suspended?

options.text: The controller stops reconciling it; manual changes stay
The chart is removed from the repository
The namespace is locked for all users

rationale: suspend stops reconciliation, so manual changes stay; resume gives control back to the declared state.

stem: What is the correct bottom-up order of the Cozystack layers?
rationale: Talos is the node OS, Kubernetes (management cluster) runs on it, and the Cozystack platform is installed on top of Kubernetes.

stem: How does Cozystack expose platform objects like tenants and VMs?

options.text: Through a separate proprietary API server unrelated to Kubernetes
As rows in an internal SQL database

rationale: Cozystack extends Kubernetes with custom resources; the dashboard and Terraform are clients of the same Kubernetes API.

stem: How does an operator change the configuration of a Talos node?

options.text: SSH to the node and edit files
Apply declarative machine configuration through the Talos API
Use the package manager on the node
Edit the root filesystem from a rescue shell

rationale: Talos has no SSH and a read-only root filesystem; the only path is declarative machine configuration through the Talos API.

stem: Why does Cozystack ship its own Talos image?

options.text: To add an SSH server for debugging
To include the DRBD and ZFS kernel modules the platform needs
To replace kubelet with a custom agent
To reduce the license cost of stock Talos

rationale: the platform needs the DRBD (LINSTOR storage) and ZFS kernel modules, which the stock Talos image does not include.

stem: Which tool is the recommended path for bootstrapping Kubernetes on Talos in Cozystack?
rationale: Talm is Cozystack's own Talos configuration manager with Helm-like templating and the documented recommended bootstrap path.

stem: In the PXE install method, which two components run as temporary Docker containers? (Choose the correct pair.)
rationale: PXE install runs Matchbox (serves the Talos image over HTTP) and dnsmasq (DHCP + TFTP) as temporary containers.

stem: How do you verify that a Cozystack installation finished successfully?

options.text: `kubectl get nodes` shows all nodes Ready
`kubectl get hr -A` shows all HelmReleases READY

rationale: the documented success check is that every platform HelmRelease shows READY True in `kubectl get hr -A`.

stem: A team wants the full Cozystack feature set, but their nodes run RKE2, not Talos. Which variant fits?
rationale: `isp-full-generic` gives the full feature set on generic distributions (k3s, kubeadm, RKE2) instead of Talos.

stem: Which variant runs on top of an existing managed Kubernetes cluster and ships **without** CNI, storage, and virtualization?
rationale: `isp-hosted` runs on an existing managed Kubernetes cluster, which already provides CNI, storage, and (if any) virtualization.

stem: What does the `default` variant contain?

options.text: The full PaaS stack with monitoring
Only PackageSources, with no preconfigured bundle
A demo tenant with sample apps

rationale: the `default` variant installs only PackageSources; the administrator enables every component manually (BYOP).

stem: How are platform packages named?
rationale: platform packages follow the `cozystack.<component>` naming, listed by `kubectl get package`.

stem: When can you disable a platform package through `bundles.disabledPackages`?

options.text: At any time; the platform removes the component automatically
Before install; removing it later requires a manual Helm operation
Never; the package set is fixed per variant

rationale: disabling works before install; removing an installed component is a manual Helm operation the platform does not do for you.

stem: Which component reconciles all platform HelmReleases?
rationale: FluxCD is the GitOps engine; every platform component is a HelmRelease that FluxCD reconciles continuously.

stem: Which component runs tenant Kubernetes control planes as pods in the management cluster?
rationale: Kamaji runs tenant Kubernetes control planes as pods inside the management cluster.

stem: Which component provides replicated block storage for persistent volumes?
rationale: LINSTOR orchestrates DRBD replicated block volumes; SeaweedFS is object storage and Velero is backup.

stem: What is the minimal documented cluster profile for a dev/lab install?

options.text: 3 nodes, 8 cores / 24 GB RAM / 50 GB + 256 GB disks each

rationale: the documented minimal profile is 3 nodes with 8 cores / 24 GB RAM and the two-disk layout (50 GB system + 256 GB data).

stem: Which network condition is strongly discouraged for a Cozystack cluster?

options.text: All nodes in one L2 segment
Round-trip time above 20 ms between nodes
Using nip.io as the platform FQDN in a lab

rationale: the latency requirement is RTT under 10 ms; above 20 ms is strongly discouraged (unsupported).

stem: What is the primary unit of isolation in Cozystack?
rationale: the Tenant CR is the "namespace with enhanced scope" — the platform's primary isolation unit.

stem: How does a tenant administrator create a sub-tenant?

options.text: By opening a support ticket to the platform team
By creating a Tenant CR, like any other catalog application
By running a Talos API command

rationale: Tenant is itself a catalog application; a sub-tenant is a Tenant CR created in the parent's namespace.

stem: Tenant `beta` is nested inside tenant `alpha`, which is under root. Which namespace does `beta` get?
rationale: ancestry accumulates (root is not repeated): root/alpha/beta -> tenant-alpha-beta.

stem: Why are dashes forbidden in tenant names?

options.text: Kubernetes forbids dashes in all resource names
The dash is the ancestry separator in derived namespace names
Dashes conflict with the Keycloak username format

rationale: the dash separates ancestor names inside the derived namespace; a dash inside a tenant name would make the ancestry ambiguous.

stem: Where do you find the tenant's own namespace in its CR?
rationale: `metadata.namespace` is the parent's namespace (where the CR lives); `status.namespace` is the namespace the platform created for the tenant itself.

stem: Which label allows a pod to reach the Kubernetes apiserver in a tenant?
rationale: the documented opt-in label is `policy.cozystack.io/allow-to-apiserver: "true"`, set per pod.

stem: How do you disable network isolation for a tenant in v1.5?

options.text: Set `isolated: false` on the Tenant CR
Delete the Cilium network policies manually
You cannot: isolation is mandatory since v1.0

rationale: the `isolated` flag was removed in v1.0; isolation is mandatory and cannot be switched off.

stem: Which component enforces tenant network isolation?
rationale: Cilium's eBPF datapath enforces the automatically generated network policies that isolate tenants.

stem: Which set lists the per-tenant service toggles?
rationale: the four per-tenant service toggles on the Tenant CR are etcd, monitoring, ingress, and seaweedfs.

stem: Tenant `beta` (inside `alpha`) has no monitoring enabled. `alpha` has `monitoring: true`. Where do beta's metrics go?

options.text: Nowhere: monitoring is off for beta
Always to the root tenant's stack

rationale: a missing service is inherited from the nearest ancestor that runs it — here the parent alpha, not necessarily root.

stem: Which preset series has a 1:4 CPU-to-RAM ratio?
rationale: preset ratios are t1=1:0.5, c1=1:1, s1=1:2, u1=1:4, m1=1:8 — the 1:4 series is u1. (This asks about tenant/app presets, not VM instance types.)

stem: With the default `cpuAllocationRatio` of 10, what does a workload with a 2-CPU limit request from the scheduler?
rationale: request = limit / cpuAllocationRatio = 2 / 10 = 0.2 CPU.

stem: A manifest sets both a preset and an explicit `resources: {cpu, memory}` block. What applies?

options.text: The preset; explicit resources are ignored
The explicit resources; they override the preset
The larger of the two values per field

rationale: explicit `resources: {cpu, memory}` values always take priority over the chosen preset.

stem: What does the documented script use to build a tenant kubeconfig?

options.text: The token, CA certificate, and server address from the tenant secret

rationale: the tenant secret holds the token, the CA certificate, and the API server address — the three parts of a kubeconfig.

stem: The platform domain is `cloud.example.com`. What is the default domain of tenant `alpha` under root?
rationale: the default tenant domain is `<name>.<parent-domain>`; alpha under root gets `alpha.cloud.example.com`.

stem: Which group of the catalog does **Qdrant** belong to?
rationale: Qdrant is a vector database — it belongs to the databases group.

stem: Which operator manages PostgreSQL in Cozystack?
rationale: CloudNativePG runs managed PostgreSQL; Strimzi is Kafka, Percona is MongoDB, Altinity is ClickHouse.

stem: How does a tenant admin create a sub-tenant?

options.text: By opening a support ticket to the platform team
By deploying the Tenant application from the catalog
By creating a Kubernetes namespace directly

rationale: Tenant is itself a catalog application; a sub-tenant is deployed like any other app, inside the parent tenant.

stem: In which API group do catalog application resources live?
rationale: all catalog applications are custom resources in `apps.cozystack.io/v1alpha1`.

stem: You create a `Postgres` CR. What does the platform create next in the chain?

options.text: A HelmRelease that installs the application chart

rationale: the chain is CR -> HelmRelease (FluxCD) -> Helm chart -> operator -> running workload.

stem: Which command shows all catalog application kinds available on the cluster?
rationale: `kubectl api-resources | grep apps.cozystack` lists every catalog kind the platform serves.

stem: What does the Cozystack dashboard create when you deploy an application from a form?

options.text: A shell script on the management node
The same custom resource that `kubectl apply` would create
A snapshot of the tenant namespace

rationale: the dashboard talks directly to the Kubernetes API; the form creates the same CR that kubectl would apply.

stem: How are the dashboard's application forms defined?

options.text: They are generated from the application resource schemas
They are hand-coded for each application by the frontend team
They are configured in the Platform Package
They are imported from Terraform modules

rationale: the dashboard is schema-driven — forms are generated from the application resource schemas, so UI and API never diverge.

stem: A team manages all infrastructure in Terraform and wants Cozystack databases in the same codebase. What is the most natural path?

options.text: Click through the dashboard and document the steps
Use the Cozystack Terraform provider or `kubernetes_manifest` resources
Write a cron job that runs kubectl

rationale: the official Terraform provider (or a plain kubernetes_manifest resource) manages the same CRs as code.

stem: What happens when you run `kubectl delete` on a `Postgres` application CR?

options.text: Only the CR object is removed; the database keeps running
The application and its workloads are removed
The command is rejected; applications can only be deleted from the dashboard
The database is archived to S3 automatically

rationale: deleting the application CR removes the whole application, including its pods and data — treat it like dropping a database.

stem: Which set of applications received TLS support in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: VPN, TCP Balancer, HTTP Cache, VPC

rationale: v1.5 added TLS for Kafka, NATS, Qdrant, and PostgreSQL; externally published databases get TLS automatically.

stem: What is the purpose of an ApplicationDefinition?

options.text: To define resource quotas for a tenant
To add a new application type to the catalog, backed by a Helm chart
To describe the network policy of an application
To pin the platform to a specific version

rationale: an ApplicationDefinition registers a new catalog application type backed by a Helm chart, with a CR kind and dashboard form.

stem: What does the `cozy-default` BackupClass in v1.5 give you?

options.text: Automatic snapshots of every virtual machine
Working managed-app backups out of the box, using a shared system S3 bucket
A full copy of the management cluster

rationale: cozy-default is the out-of-the-box BackupClass wired to a shared system S3 bucket (full model in M6).

stem: How does KubeVirt run a virtual machine?

options.text: On a separate hypervisor cluster next to Kubernetes
Inside a Kubernetes pod, as a qemu process
As a WebAssembly module in the kubelet
Inside a Docker-in-Docker container on the control plane

rationale: KubeVirt runs each VM as a qemu/KVM process inside a pod, so the VM is a normal Kubernetes workload.

stem: What is the role of CDI in the virtualization stack?

options.text: It schedules VM pods across nodes
It provides the VNC console for VMs
It imports disk images into persistent volumes
It replicates disks between data centers

rationale: CDI (Containerized Data Importer) fills PVCs with disk images — from URLs, registries, or uploads — via DataVolume objects.

stem: Which statement about VMs in Cozystack is correct?

options.text: VMs are excluded from tenant quotas
VMs need a dedicated, separate scheduler service
VMs are placed by the standard Kubernetes scheduler

rationale: because a VM is a pod, the standard scheduler places it, and quotas and network policies apply to it.

stem: What is the canonical way to create a virtual machine in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: Create a single VirtualMachine resource with an inline disk
Create a VMDisk first, then a VMInstance that references it
Create a VMInstance first; the platform creates disks automatically
Create a DataVolume and a Pod manually

rationale: the canonical v1.5 model is two CRs, disk first: VMDisk (storage), then VMInstance referencing it.

stem: Why are the disk and the instance separate resources?

options.text: Kubernetes cannot store two specifications in one object
The disk lifecycle is independent: data can survive instance deletion and disks can be reused
Disks and instances must run in different namespaces
It is required for live migration

rationale: separate lifecycles are the point — a disk survives instance deletion, can be re-attached and backed up on its own.

stem: A team wants every new VM to start from the same prepared Ubuntu image, without downloading it each time. What should they use?

options.text: A VMImage (golden image) as the disk source
The upload source with a shared laptop

rationale: a VMImage is the golden image: publish once, then clone new disks from it with source.image.name.

stem: A Linux VM boots, but its network configuration is broken and SSH does not work. Which access method still works?
rationale: the serial console does not depend on guest networking — it is the last-resort access path.

stem: What does cloud-init do?

options.text: It replicates VM disks across nodes
It configures the guest OS at first boot: users, SSH keys, packages
It schedules the VM pod onto a node
It converts disk images between formats

rationale: cloud-init runs at first boot inside the guest and applies users, keys, hostname, and packages.

stem: Which feature exists in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: Automatic restart of VMs after host failure (vSphere HA equivalent)
Continuous automatic VM rebalancing across nodes (DRS equivalent)
Live migration of running VMs between nodes

rationale: live migration exists; HA auto-restart, DRS rebalancing, and CBT backups are honest gaps of v1.5.

stem: A team asks: "If a node dies, will our VMs restart on another node automatically?" What is the honest v1.5 answer?

options.text: Yes, KubeVirt restarts them within seconds
No — there is no fencing-based auto-restart out of the box; recovery includes manual steps
Yes, but only for Windows guests

rationale: there is no fencing-based auto-restart in v1.5; node-failure recovery for VMs includes manual steps.

stem: What changed for GPU passthrough in v1.5?

options.text: GPUs can no longer be attached to VMs
Node preparation was automated: GPU node labeling and device binding
GPU passthrough now requires a commercial license
GPUs are shared between VMs by default

rationale: v1.5 automated GPU node preparation: labeling and vfio-pci device binding; a VMInstance requests a GPU via its gpus field.

stem: Which component enforces tenant network isolation in Cozystack?
rationale: Cilium enforces the automatically generated network policies that isolate tenants (M2).

stem: A pod inside a tenant must call the Kubernetes API server. What is required?

options.text: Nothing; API access is open by default
Setting `isolated: false` on the Tenant resource

rationale: API server access is closed by default; the pod opts in with the `policy.cozystack.io/allow-to-apiserver: "true"` label.

stem: Which property does Kube-OVN add to the platform?

options.text: Stable pod IP addresses across rescheduling

rationale: Kube-OVN's centralized IPAM keeps a pod's IP across rescheduling; the other options belong to TenantGateway/cert-manager, Cilium, and ExternalDNS.

stem: Why are stable IP addresses especially important for virtual machines?

options.text: Kubernetes forbids IP changes for pods
Guest workloads, firewall rules, and licenses often depend on a fixed IP

rationale: guests, firewall rules, and licenses often pin to an IP; a VM that changed IP on every migration would break them.

stem: A colleague asks which CNI layer does what. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Cilium: overlay and IPAM; Kube-OVN: network policies
Cilium: policies and Services (eBPF); Kube-OVN: overlay, centralized IPAM, stable IPs, VPC
Both layers do the same job for redundancy

rationale: the two CNIs cooperate: Cilium handles packet processing, Services, and policies; Kube-OVN handles the overlay, IPAM, stable IPs, and VPC.

stem: What happens to a `LoadBalancer` Service on a bare-metal cluster **without** MetalLB?

options.text: It gets an IP from the pod network
Its external IP stays pending forever
It falls back to NodePort automatically
It is rejected by the API server

rationale: on bare metal nothing supplies external IPs; without MetalLB the Service's external IP stays pending.

stem: Which statement describes MetalLB's BGP mode?

options.text: One node answers ARP requests for the service IP
Nodes announce service IPs to physical routers as routes
It works only in public clouds

rationale: in BGP mode nodes peer with physical routers and announce service IPs as routes (FRR-K8s backend since v1.5); ARP answering is L2 mode.

stem: How is ingress deployed in Cozystack?

options.text: One shared ingress controller for the whole platform
One ingress-nginx controller per tenant, enabled by a tenant toggle
Ingress runs on a dedicated hardware appliance
Ingress is not supported; only LoadBalancer Services exist

rationale: ingress-nginx is deployed per tenant via the `ingress` toggle; missing services are inherited from the parent (M2).

stem: What backs the TenantGateway data plane?
rationale: TenantGateway is Gateway API implemented by Cilium — no nginx in that data path.

stem: A tenant needs a wildcard certificate for `*.apps.example.com`. Which validation mode supports this?
rationale: wildcard certificates require DNS-01 validation; HTTP-01 cannot issue wildcards.

stem: The platform domain is `cloud.example.com`. What is the default domain of tenant `alpha` created directly under root?
rationale: the default tenant domain is `<name>.<parent-domain>`, so alpha under root gets `alpha.cloud.example.com`.

stem: Which component creates DNS records for published applications automatically?
rationale: ExternalDNS watches published services/ingresses and creates DNS records; cert-manager handles certificates, not names.

stem: Which component stores metrics in Cozystack?
rationale: VictoriaMetrics (VMCluster) stores metrics; there is no Prometheus in the stack, only PromQL compatibility.

stem: A tenant has no Monitoring application of its own. What happens when its workloads need monitoring?

options.text: The tenant must install Prometheus manually
The tenant inherits the monitoring service from its parent tenant
The platform blocks new workloads in this tenant

rationale: Monitoring is a per-tenant catalog application; a tenant without its own inherits the nearest ancestor's (M2 inheritance rule).

stem: Which component groups and deduplicates alerts before sending notifications?
rationale: the pipeline is VMAlert (evaluates rules) -> Alerta (groups, deduplicates, routes) -> Email/SMS/Slack.

stem: You want to check the health of LINSTOR volumes. Which standard dashboard group do you open?
rationale: the Storage dashboard group covers LINSTOR and SeaweedFS health.

stem: A user wants an automatic backup of a managed PostgreSQL database every night. Which object do they create?
rationale: a Plan is the scheduled backup (cron); a BackupJob is a one-off run; a Backup is the result object.

stem: Which object is cluster-scoped and created by the platform administrator?
rationale: BackupClass is the single cluster-scoped configuration object created by the platform administrator; the rest are user- or system-created.

stem: What does the `cozy-default` BackupClass in v1.5 provide?

options.text: Automatic backups of the whole management cluster
A ready backup configuration with a shared system S3 bucket, so managed-app backups work without admin setup
A free external S3 account for every tenant

rationale: cozy-default ships since v1.5 with a shared system S3 bucket, so managed-app backups work without administrator setup.

stem: Since which release is Velero a default Cozystack component?
rationale: Velero (cozystack.velero) became a default platform component in v1.5.

stem: Which Velero object defines *where* backups are stored?
rationale: the BackupStorageLocation defines the S3 target where backups land; Strategies define how, BackupClass binds them to app types.

stem: Which items are NOT captured by a managed-app data-only backup? (Choose the best answer.)

options.text: Helm release, application CR, and operator secrets

rationale: data-only backups capture the database content; the Helm release, application CR, and operator secrets are not captured.

stem: What must be true before you restore a managed-app backup?

options.text: The target application must already be provisioned
The tenant must be deleted first

rationale: restore fills an existing database with data; because backups are data-only, the target application must already be provisioned.

stem: What kind of VM backups does the platform make?

options.text: Full backups of configuration and all attached disks

rationale: a VM backup captures the configuration plus all attached disks, and every backup is full — no CBT/incrementals exist.

stem: What does a Kubernetes controller do?

options.text: It runs user commands one by one, in order
It continuously compares desired state with actual state and acts on the difference
It stores the cluster configuration on disk
It routes network traffic between pods

rationale: a controller runs the reconciliation loop: compare desired with actual state and act on the difference, forever.

stem: Which object provides a stable network name in front of a set of pods?
rationale: a Service gives a stable name and virtual IP in front of a changing set of pods.

stem: Why does `kubectl get tenants` work on a Cozystack cluster?

options.text: Tenants are a built-in Kubernetes object type
Cozystack extends the Kubernetes API, so the API server knows the Tenant type (served by the cozystack-api aggregated server)
kubectl has a special Cozystack plugin
It only works inside the dashboard terminal

rationale: Cozystack extends the Kubernetes API — apps.cozystack.io kinds are served by the cozystack-api aggregated API server, so standard kubectl verbs work.

stem: Which API group contains the Cozystack catalog resources?
rationale: all catalog resources — Tenant, Postgres, VMInstance, and the rest — live in apps.cozystack.io/v1alpha1.

stem: What is the first diagnostic command to check overall Cozystack platform health?
rationale: every platform component is a HelmRelease, so `kubectl get hr -A` with all READY True is the universal health check.

stem: What does a HelmRelease object declare?

options.text: A one-time installation command that runs once and disappears
That a specific chart with specific values must be installed and kept installed
A backup of a Helm chart
The Git repository where application source code lives

rationale: a HelmRelease declares desired state — chart, version, values — and FluxCD keeps it installed and reconciled.

stem: What is a Helm chart?

options.text: A running instance of an application
A package of Kubernetes manifest templates plus metadata

rationale: a chart is the package (templates + metadata); a release is that chart installed with specific values.

stem: How is the Cozystack platform itself installed?

options.text: With an operating system package manager (apt/yum)
By copying binaries to every node over SSH
With a Helm command that installs the cozy-installer chart

rationale: the platform installs with one idempotent Helm command: `helm upgrade --install ... cozy-installer` into cozy-system (M1).
